subjects.displayTitle: Love and longing: the ache of nearness
subjects.introduction: Every night consumed by the fire of separation, every morning gladdened by fresh tokens of bounty: Bahá’u’lláh describes the lover of God as someone who weeps and laughs within the same day and is not ashamed of either. Longing of this kind is not a problem to be solved. It is the moth throwing itself against the flame with no thought of benefit, the fish that is never sated with water, the lover for whom a thousand years before the beloved’s face pass like an hour. Yet the same Writings issue a searching warning: love itself can become a veil, and whoever cherishes a remembered sign of the Beloved may fail to recognize the living sun when it moves on. The night search of the Song of Solomon, in which the lover leaves her bed, questions the watchmen and at last finds the one her soul loves, gives this restlessness a human voice to set beside the prayers and poems [1]. Grief under persecution and the ache of bereavement speak here too, each asking to be read with care for the person and the hour. The journey continues into love understood as fire, and into the love of God that seeks the Beloved beyond every consolation it might receive.
subjects.arc: Enter through hope within sorrow, explore the language of longing and its veils, and return through prayer to mercy and enduring love.

order.why: Ask whether even love can become a veil.
shortened: 34 This is the realm of pure awareness and utter self-effacement. Not even love can find a way to this plane, nor doth affection have a place therein. Wherefore is it said: "Love is a veil betwixt the lover and the beloved." Here love becometh but an obstructing veil, and aught save the Friend but a curtain.

order.why: Open with grief and hope held together.
shortened: O my God! Every night I am consumed by the fire of separation from Thee, and every day I am gladdened by the wondrous tokens of Thy bounty. In the night-time I weep in my despair at being remote from the evidences of Thy triumph and Thy loving-kindness, and in the daytime I laugh with hope at the wondrous manifestations of Thy generosity and benevolence.

order.why: Introduce the transformation of bitterness through love.
shortened: Through divine love every bitterness will become sweet: the colocynth will turn to sweet honey, the fang of a snake to medicine, poison to an antidote for them that have minds to know, calamity to comfort, hardships will become blessings, cruelty will turn to fidelity and affliction to pleasure.

order.why: Hear the related warning in the Seven Valleys.
shortened: 32 Nay, they would even soar above this station, as it is said: "Love is a veil betwixt the lover and beloved." "More than this I am not permitted to tell."

order.why: Distinguish the remembered sign from the living sun.
Keep knowledge and yearning in conversation.
shortened: Despite my recognition of all this and my certitude in all that Thou hast taught me of the wonders of the craftsmanship of Thy heavens of ordainment, the ornaments of the movements of the cycles of Thy sovereign handiwork, and the revolutions of the pillars of the manifestations of Thy glorious might, I am consumed by the fire whose ember sets ablaze all existence, and I weep tears from which all the seas find their essence.

order.why: Consider the moth’s love beyond personal benefit.
shortened: A moth loves the light, though his wings are burnt. Though his wings are singed, he throws himself against the flame. He does not love the light because it has conferred some benefit upon him. Therefore he hovers round the light, though he sacrifices his wings.
This is the highest degree of love. Without this abandonment, this ecstacy, love is imperfect.
The lover of God loves Him for Himself, not for his own sake.

order.why: Read the moth image in its devotional register.
Join burning desire with dependence on mercy.
Uses the pain of love to express longing for the Beloved.
Hear the collective prayer within that imagery.
shortened: Praise be to God, the loved ones of that region are intoxicated with the overflowing cup and delighted by witnessing the lights. They are enkindled by the ignited fire of love for the Ancient Beauty and, like moths to the candle of love, have burned their wings.
O Lord! Increase their burning, their longing, and their radiance.

order.why: Follow the analogy from human passion toward divine love.
shortened: O thou true Friend! Love requireth man to sacrifice his life for his beloved, become a wanderer and fully enamoured, accept public disgrace, abandon name and trace, and forget body and soul for love's sake. Such is the requirement of love in the contingent world; consider then what the love of God and passionate devotion to the Celestial Beloved would require!

order.why: Introduce the fish’s unending need for water.
Ask why even union can intensify longing.
shortened: I discover in my heart such rapture from the ardor of union with Thee and longing to meet Thee that I find no patience in separation from Thee nor composure in attaining Thee. It is as though I know not what I desire of Thee - if I seek union through the wonders of Thy favors, I witness that in union with Thee my cries are raised and my voice is lifted up; and if I show patience in separation from Thee, I witness that in Thy remoteness my spirit departs and my soul finds no rest ever.

order.why: Consider the particular pain of lost nearness.
Hear a second expression of that loss.
Hold nearness and distance in the same yearning.
Read the language of Layla and the lovers.
Let the memorial’s poems introduce another literary voice.
shortened: And so as he wandered through the long dark nights, Ustad would sing these lines:
I am lost, O Love, possessed and dazed,
Love's fool am I, in all the earth.
They call me first among the crazed,
Though I once came first for wit and worth.
O Love, who sellest me this wine,
O Love, for whom I burn and bleed,
Love, for whom I cry and pine--
Thou the Piper, I the reed.

order.why: Hear renewal through mercy in the poem.
Read the cited poet’s acceptance of what transpires.
Keep poison and healing within poetic paradox.
Read the poem’s love and wrath together.
Hear wounds and balm as devotional images.
Consider anguish described as a sweet draught.
shortened: They have created the world compounded of honey and colocynth. How can the heartless one draw a peaceful breath in this dusty realm of water and clay, or spread the couch of repose? If it offers a sweet draught to the lip, it draws forth a cry of anguish from the soul.

order.why: Read delight and torment within the same utterance.
Approach the imagery of the Beloved’s hair.
Consider that image as both attraction and obstacle.
Follow the wandering prompted by the divine Beloved.
Read the woman’s longing through Joseph imagery.
Consider beauty concealed behind the veil.
Hear the alternation of yearning and concealment.
Read the paradox of love kindled and presence withheld.
shortened: Thou art He Who, O my God, hath kindled my heart with Thy love, then forbidden me from beholding Thy beauty, and Who hath caused my heart to melt in passion and yearning for Thee, then prevented me from entering the sanctuary of Thy nearness and attaining Thy presence.

order.why: Let the complaint of banishment remain audible.
shortened: Shouldst thou desire to know Me, then know of a certainty that I am He Who depriveth the yearning ones of entrance into the court of My holiness, and banisheth them far from the seat of My throne. I am He Who hath consumed the hearts of lovers in the fire of separation, and abandoned them in the wildernesses of the earth.

order.why: Hear Maryam addressed amid the lover’s grief.
shortened: The lover's eyes must be wet, whereat the Beloved may coyly flash an amorous glance. If the lover crieth out a hundred words of grief, the Beloved but turneth more away.

order.why: Keep the prayer within its context of bereavement.
Read the plea arising from remoteness with care.
Place a prayer for comfort beside that anguish.
Keep the ironic language of brotherly love in its troubled context.
shortened: All these affairs are from the efforts of the aforementioned brother and in truth his effort is appreciated, for it has caused us to drink a bitter cup and taste deadly poison in divine love with every breath.

order.why: Consider fidelity amid blame and tests.
Read the language of persecution and chains.
Hear self-effacement in its mystical register.
shortened: This is the arena of self-annihilation, of a hundred thousand acts of self -immolation, of being melted in pure love.

order.why: Read the lover’s offering of life.
Keep the intense language of suffering attributed to its source.
shortened: From the outset love was rebellious and bloodthirsty,
So as to put every stranger to flight.

One of the requisites of true love is willingness to bear every suffering and tribulation that hath occurred in the past or may occur in the future. Hence a passionate lover is always stained with blood, and he that yearneth to meet the Beloved a constant wanderer.

order.why: Hear the prayer’s homelessness and bewilderment.
Consider the breaking of patience and composure.
Read the festival through one voice’s sorrow.
Hear helplessness expressed in verse.
shortened:
The helpless heart becomes lament, with many sighs and many cries,
Afflicted and without a cure, yet every moment sacrifice.

order.why: Let exhaustion and tears retain their full weight.
shortened: My eyes have turned white from flowing tears - illuminate them with the collyrium of Thy bounty.
O Lord! No occupation remains for me - I have become powerless, hopeless, with burning entrails, confined on all sides, with broken bonds and scattered desires.

order.why: Consider longing intensified by inability to hear.
shortened: Tears flow from my eyes, sighs rise from my heart, and regrets appear in my soul from being separated from beholding the lights of Thy beauty and being deprived of hearing Thy utterance.

order.why: Read tears as the language of prayer.
shortened: Verily, Thou art witnessing that the fire is ablaze in the breasts, the tears are streaming from the eyes and the period of patience and silence hath come to an end. The eyes of the beloved ones, O my God, are swimming in tears; the hearts of the yearning ones, O my Beloved, are wandering in the wilderness of Thy mercifulness; and the souls of the attracted ones, O my Desire, are afflicted with anguish on account of Thy separation!

order.why: Hear the supplication under separation.
shortened: My God, my God! You see me aflame with the fire of Your love, bereft of patience from separation from Your heavenly presence, tears flowing from being deprived of Your holy court, my heart burning and my gathering scattered, disheveled and dust-covered from falling upon the earth of abasement in the desert of separation from You.

order.why: Read the plea against the burden of remoteness.
Consider the arrows of separation as an image.
shortened: Were anyone to search the hearts of Thy lovers, they would find them pierced by the arrows of separation from Thee, and their innermost beings aflame with the fire of remoteness from Thee.

order.why: Hear longing spread through the whole person.
Read the heart’s agitation.
Turn impatience into a direct petition.
shortened: The fire of Your love burns in his heart, his patience is exhausted from longing to attain Your presence, and his tears flow from yearning to witness Your beauty.

order.why: Consider remembrance that cannot be suppressed.
shortened: And if I restrain the tongue from the wondrous utterances in describing Thee, by Thy might my heart raiseth the banners of Thy remembrance, and if I withhold the heart from what it experienceth lest anyone discover my love for Thee, by Thy beauty my spirit soareth in the heaven of Thy nearness and wingeth its flight in the atmosphere of reunion with Thee, and if I prevent my feet from walking in Thy path, I witness that hands are raised toward the garden of Thy glory and the city of meeting with Thee.

order.why: Follow longing into the act of writing.
Read pain as the melody of pen and lamp.
shortened: The well-guarded secrets in this day are the mysteries of the love of God, which are hidden in the innermost essence of the human heart. Its fire ignites all hearts and its heat encompasses all regions. At one time this mystery is felt through the aching pangs of love; at another it expresses itself through the words of a pen, at a third time it may be a melody that ignites the very life within the soul, and yet again it is a lamp that might set ablaze the universe.

order.why: Hear the cosmic scale of the lament.
Let the dialogue within the heart offer consolation.
shortened:
Verily, the intensity of her sorrows maketh Me weep and causeth My
heart to address her, saying: Understand thou well the heat which is consuming
Me that thou mayest praise God for thy plight, and thy soul may
find abundant joy. And My liver addresseth My heart saying: Wert thou to
be informed of how I burn and blaze, thou wouldst find the fire thou art
in to be light and cold.

order.why: Rest in the assurance that longing is known.
shortened: O my God! Thou knowest the yearning of the lovers in their separation and remoteness from Thee, and the sighs of them that long for Thee when prevented from turning to the heaven of Thy grace.

order.why: Read the loving response to a letter.
shortened: O thou who art enkindled with the fire of the love of God! The marks of thy pen indicating the burning fire of longing and complaint of the burning fire of separation were observed with eagerness and love.

order.why: Hear the answering call of presence.
Join remembrance with a plea for reunion.
shortened: I behold that my remembrance, for all its loftiness and sovereignty, lieth prostrate upon the dust, crying out: "O Lord of Lords! Thou seest how my heart hath melted in my separation from Thee - have I any portion of the ocean of Thy reunion? Thou seest how I am utterly consumed by the fire of remoteness and estrangement from Thee - have I any share of the light of Thy nearness and meeting with Thee?"

order.why: Turn thirst toward the water of the Face.
Read the extended prayer for healing and reunion.
shortened: O maid-servant of God! verily, I long for that cup, which is overflowing with the bounty of God, as a patient desiring to be healed, as a thirsty soul seeking water, as the poor in quest of wealth, and as one in separation yearning after the meeting of the beloved one night and day.

order.why: Consider the intoxicating image of one drop.
shortened: It seems the gates of hope have closed and the gardens of despair have opened. A world lies unconscious from the sweet wine of reunion, while these emigrants cry out for but a drop.

order.why: Return to sweetness discovered in adversity.
shortened: Every hair of my head proclaimeth: "But for the adversities that befall me in Thy path, how could I ever taste the divine sweetness of Thy tenderness and love?"

order.why: Hear remembrance sustained in exile.
Distinguish separation from other causes of sorrow.
Close with a prayer for good in both worlds.
shortened: I beseech Thee, O my God, by the standards of Thy guidance and the banners of Thy utterance, and by the hearts which have been set ablaze with the fire of separation from Thee in Thy days, and by the tears of the lovers throughout all regions, and by the appearance of Thy Cause on the Day of the Covenant, to ordain for me from Thy Most Glorious Pen the good of the world to come and of this world.

questions: How do the opening passages make room for hope without diminishing sorrow?
What changes when a passage is read as a mystical poem, a prayer under persecution, or an expression of bereavement?
How might a cherished image of the Beloved become a veil, and what would recognition beyond that image involve?
What do the recurring images of thirst, fire, and fragrance reveal about the limits of ordinary descriptions of love?
How does the night search in the Song of Solomon illuminate these readings, and what differences in voice and setting matter?
What forms of fidelity, compassion, or service might emerge from longing that seeks more than its own consolation?

references.label: 1 · Song of Solomon 3:1–4 · Searching through the night
references.note: In the King James Version, a lover searches at night, goes into the city, questions the watchmen, and finally finds the beloved. Compare the movement from absence to encounter with the compilation’s prayers and poems of longing. The biblical passage gives a human lover’s voice; considering its resonances with devotional longing need not erase that voice or its particular setting.

subjects.displayTitle: Cultivating character: effort, joy, and service
subjects.introduction: We are tender plants in Thy garden, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá prays; make us trees laden with fruit. The work of character starts from that confidence that something is already planted, and then asks for effort: look within to find your own errors, tear down the weak point, and build a good quality in the place where the bad one stood. The same counsel refuses morbidity. Spend your time on what brings joy to heart and soul, do not be occupied with your failings, and remember that mistakes are how a person learns and unfolds the higher self within. Aristotle’s observation that we become just by doing just acts names the habituation that runs under these teachings, though here prayer and grace do work that habit alone cannot [1]. And the purpose is never private: refine your own soul, Bahá’u’lláh says, and then arise to reform others. The road leads on into bringing oneself to account each day, the education of capacity, the discipline of mindfulness, and the fruit by which a tree is known.
subjects.arc: Begin with capacity and encouragement, move into the practices of self-examination and renewal, and let personal discipline bear fruit in service.

order.why: Seek the development of every quality.
Open with the prayer for unrealized capacities.
Place kindness to prisoners near the beginning.
shortened: Convey on my behalf to the two prisoners in San Quentin the utmost kindness, and tell them: "That prison in the sight of wise souls is a school of training and development. Ye must strive with heart and soul that ye may become renowned in character and knowledge."

order.why: Introduce the upward purpose of true self-love.
shortened: The true love of self is that which leads forward and upward in a direct course toward higher life and being.

order.why: Give joy and renewed strength an early place.
Balance scrutiny with freedom from fixation on failure.
Read tests as revealing strengths as well as weaknesses.
shortened: Tests reveal strength as well as weakness and provide opportunity to remedy defects.

The soul also becomes aware of its strength, a former weakness is overcome and a surprise awaits the soul; it realizes its growth, and so the heavy discipline is proved to be nutritive and a new confidence and trust is born in the consciousness, and this leads to mastery, self-discipline becomes self-mastery.

order.why: Allow mistakes a place in learning.
shortened: When the believers are insistent, Abdul Baha must give them answers, and it is their wish always that Abdul Baha grants them. He knows what their wish in reality is. They must make mistakes to learn, and to unfold the higher which is within themselves.

order.why: Move from discarding faults to developing replacements.
shortened: Each man must look to himself and within himself to find his errors and weaknesses.

When we find weak points in our character we must begin to tear down; and also we must not neglect to build up good qualities in place of the evil ones which we discard. It is a law of our nature that to remove a characteristic permanently another must be developed in its stead.

order.why: Connect intention and effort with latent qualities.
shortened: Thus, through the restoring waters of pure intention and unselfish effort, the earth of human potentialities will blossom with its own latent excellence and flower into praiseworthy qualities, and bear and flourish until it comes to rival that rosegarden of knowledge which belonged to our forefathers.

order.why: Read the concise answer on each quality’s function.
Keep the horizon of improvement open.
shortened: No matter what level a human being reaches, he can still attain higher ones, so he is always making effort and desiring more.

order.why: Make daily progress concrete.
shortened: His aim must be to rise day unto day in the scale of divine and human virtues; his today be better than yesterday and his tomorrow better than today.

order.why: Begin education with oneself.
shortened: Every person should first think about their own education, should think about perfecting themselves, for self-education is primary.

order.why: Consider responsibility before correcting others.
shortened: You ought first to be perfect, then to think about the perfections of others. Until you are perfect you cannot make others perfect; until you are rich you cannot make others rich; until you are alive you cannot give life to others.

order.why: Read the related call to examine one’s faults.
shortened: As long as a soul is not perfected how can he efface the defects of others? Unless he is detached from aught else save God how can he teach severance to others?

order.why: Test knowledge in personal practice.
Join personal refinement with helping others.
shortened: All must occupy themselves with the refinement of their own souls and thereafter arise for the reformation of others.

order.why: Return to conduct as the immediate task.
shortened: Today, every soul must occupy himself with his own reformation, and manifest pure deeds and praiseworthy, acceptable conduct.

order.why: Hear the challenge to self-satisfaction.
Read the reported warning against complacency.
shortened: The person who is satisfied with himself is the manifestation of Satan and the one who is not satisfied is the manifestation of the Merciful One. An egotist does not progress but the one who thinks himself imperfect will seek perfection for himself and will progress.

order.why: Consider the danger of unrecognized shortcomings.
shortened: If a person does not sense the same, remains unaware of his shortcomings, exerts no efforts to improve himself, then he is no better than a stone.

order.why: Turn praise toward others.
Read Abdu’l-Baha’s humility in its devotional voice.
shortened: In any case, 'Abdu'l-Baha undertakes this perilous journey with the hope that perhaps he may find some relief from intense shame and seek deliverance from embarrassment, for until now he has not drawn a single breath in servitude to the Sacred Threshold nor rendered any service to the servants of the Blessed Beauty. Perhaps during this absence divine aid and favor will arrive and he may take a step on the path of His good-pleasure.

order.why: Explore the glass case as an image of self-knowledge.
Consider the polishing of a jewel.
shortened: Say: O friends! Strive that the jewels of human beings may become manifest and evident through the burnishing of divine grace.

order.why: Read remembrance as cultivation and weeding.
Hear the prayer for release from deception.
shortened: Purge out, then, from them, O my God, all doubts and idle fancies, and sanctify them from whatsoever becometh not their kinship with Thee, O Thou Who art the Lord of names, and the Source of utterance.

order.why: Consider the moral work of governing oneself.
Consider the heart’s governance of passion.
Reconsider courage through mastery of self.
Distinguish bodily strength from freedom within.
shortened: Physical champions and earthly men, although outwardly possessing strength and power, are yet captives of desire and passion, and are caught and debased by the lowest of things.

order.why: Join spiritual advancement with restraint and forgiveness.
shortened: When the wayfarer reaches this most exalted and supreme station, firstly no anger arises in him that he should need to suppress it, and no self remains that should need to forgive.

order.why: Read the particular counsel to youth.
Keep the reported severe language within its educational context.
shortened: The life of man is useful if he attains the perfections of man. If he becomes the center of the imperfections of the world of humanity, death is better than life, and nonexistence better than existence. Therefore, make ye an effort in order that these children may be rightly trained and educated and that each one of them may attain perfection in the world of humanity.

order.why: Read the historical exhortation without turning it into a diagnosis.
Keep the reported discussion of endurance in its particular context.
Consider the reported emphasis on resolve.
Read the reported counsel on appetite as situated advice.
shortened: Even food should only be for meeting needs - excess beyond necessity leads to depression, listlessness and ultimately to illness and affliction.

order.why: Keep the personal example of simple living distinct.
Retain the reported example of practiced physical skill.
Turn from entanglement toward renewed simplicity.
Read the disappointment over a refused opportunity.
Consider counsel sent to prompt reflection.
Hear the instruction to cultivate character quietly.
shortened: For now, in that land, make silence and quietude your course of action and occupy yourself with the cultivation of virtuous character and the improvement of conditions.

order.why: Read striving in the arena of divine knowledge.
shortened: This being so, strive to become a man of the arena of divine knowledge and a luminous star in the heaven.

order.why: Return to the continuing work of study.
Consider good intention as a beginning.
Join moral progress with guidance.
Read devotion as steady practice.
shortened: Devotion to one's calling, effort in its speedy execution, simplicity of sprit and steadfastness through all the ups and downs, these are the hallmarks of success.

order.why: Hold outward and inward perfections together.
shortened: Night and day think on acquiring outer and inner perfections, and day and night draw illumination from pure springs so that through the grace of the Ancient Beauty each of you may become, in all conditions, a great sign of the Most Glorious Beauty and the manifestation of one of the names of the Self-Subsisting, Ever-Living Lord.

order.why: Consider their fruit across days and nights.
shortened: Assuredly, neglect not, throughout thy days and nights, the acquisition of spiritual and outward perfections, that the fruits of existence may be made manifest through thee. This is the counsel and testament of a faithful counselor.

order.why: Carry qualities into work, arts, and sciences.
shortened: Man must work and in that work show the qualities of GOD and thus do good. His work, both material and spiritual, must show what he is. By his arts, sciences, inventions and all of his work he must show his best ability.

order.why: Make room for originality and expansive ideals.
shortened: Be ye the fruit-bearing trees of the garden of Abha, the shining lamps in the gathering of the friends, the fragrant flowers of the meadows of the world and the efficient members of the body polity.
Be ye original, invent your thoughts and deeds. Do not let the sphere of your ideals be contracted. Be not imitators. Seek the radiant path of Divine Glory. Be ye attracted and enkindled.

order.why: Turn personal effort toward the public good.
Read the chain from humility to social service.
Join overcoming self with charitable action.
Let good works embody the claim.
shortened: Man must become the educative origin of divine perfections. Man must become the embodiment of good works. Man must become the means of the wellbeing and prosperity of the commonwealth of humanity.

order.why: Consider virtues that adorn human life.
Read inherited examples as an invitation to conduct.
Keep the praise of youthful excellence in context.
shortened: This is the cause of eternal glory, this is the cause of the adornment of human reality, and this is what befitteth the youth in this glorious century. This is what beseeming those who are young in this sacred epoch.

order.why: Hear encouragement to acquire human perfections.
Describes disciplined religious practice as a means of developing moral virtues.
Read service as a source of renewed hope.
shortened: The friends must show determination and display strength and might in the field of His service, and win the ball of precedence, so that this withered and dejected soul of Abdul-Baha may find spirit and fragrance and become hopeful.

order.why: Hear the prayer for continuing acceptance and progress.
shortened: I hope therefore that at the Divine Threshold thou mayest secure favor, may become connected with the Kingdom by ideal ties and may daily progress so that thou mayest be accepted in the Sight of His Holiness Baha'u'llah!

order.why: Contrast living humanity with a merely sculptured form.
shortened: Therefore, strive to become true human beings who attain their heart's desire, not merely sculptured idols of Farkhar.

order.why: Gather the appeal into highest excellence.
shortened: Strive thou, therefore, to become a dawning-place of highest excellence.

order.why: Retain the concise reported call to eager progress.
shortened: "Endeavor and strive eagerly that you may progress and advance rapidly. You are born in this holy day, attaining this great privilege by the favor of God, therefore you must not waste or throw away this bounty and mercy.

order.why: Connect deeds with the elevation of the Cause.
shortened: This Wronged One counsels the friends of God to perform such deeds as will conduce to the exaltation of His Cause and the elevation of His Word amongst His servants.

order.why: Read commands as guidance beyond appetite.
shortened: We have commanded all to that which shall preserve them from the promptings of self and passion and draw them nigh unto God, the Lord of the Day of Return.

order.why: Consider counsel grounded in the counselor’s own practice.
shortened: Keep thyself from self and be not neglectful in the Cause of God. Be in the utmost state of submission and contentment, and follow not thy desires but rather follow what this needy servant conveyeth unto thee, for he desireth for thee naught save what he desireth for himself, and teacheth thee not a letter except by that which he hath taught himself, and remembereth thee not save by that which he remembereth his own soul, and loveth thee now as he loved thee before.

order.why: Return to character that illuminates others.
shortened: If you follow My way, verily He will guide you to the straight path. Whoso is adorned with the ornament of My character traits verily shines forth in the kingdom and by him the horizons are illumined.

order.why: End with enthusiasm for acquiring virtues.

questions: How do the images of cultivation, polishing, and clearing glass offer different understandings of personal growth?
How can honest self-examination coexist with joy and freedom from excessive preoccupation with one’s faults?
What would it mean to develop a positive quality in place of a habit one hopes to leave behind?
How does Aristotle’s account of repeated action illuminate these readings, and what additional roles do prayer and divine assistance play here?
What distinctions matter when applying a general principle, personal advice, or a reported example from a particular life?
How might daily self-accounting become visible in greater usefulness, kindness, or service to others?

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 · Character through practice
references.note: In W. D. Ross’s translation, Aristotle connects moral virtue with habituation: people develop their dispositions through the kinds of acts they repeatedly perform. He compares moral learning with acquiring a craft and emphasizes the importance of early habits. Read this beside the compilation’s concern with replacing faults, educating oneself, and translating knowledge into action, while considering the distinct place given here to prayer, love, and grace.

subjects.displayTitle: Two civilizations: the lamp and its light
subjects.introduction: Material civilization, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, is the lamp, and spiritual civilization is the light within it; one is a beautiful body and the other the spirit of life, and a bird with a single wing cannot fly. He admired the telephone and the railway, and He saw in the same hour battleships that could level a city, proof that in material progress good and evil advance together unless something directs them. Bahá’u’lláh commanded the pursuit of useful sciences, commerce, industry and agriculture, yet He declared that all have been created for the betterment of the world. Just government carries the one call to prosperity and the Word of God the other; a mother who tells her child to study hard and become a general, but never to become just and sincere, has answered only half of it. Confucius drew a kindred line between people who merely avoid punishment and people led by virtue into moral awareness [1]. The way onward passes through the exchange between East and West, the temptations of materialism, and the continual ascent of civilization itself.
subjects.arc: Begin with the lamp and the purpose of power, join practical development to moral education, and consider the institutions and habits of a shared civilization.

order.why: Open with the lamp, its light, and two wings.
shortened: Material civilization is like unto the lamp, while spiritual civilization is the light in that lamp. If the material and spiritual civilization become united, then we will have the light and the lamp together, and the outcome will be perfect. For material civilization is like unto a beautiful body, and spiritual civilization is like unto the spirit of life.

For man two wings are necessary. One wing is physical power and material civilization; the other is spiritual power and divine civilization. With one wing only, flight is impossible. Two wings are essential. Therefore, no matter how much material civilization advances, it cannot attain to perfection except through the uplift of spiritual civilization.

order.why: Ask what directs the growth of technical power.
shortened: No matter how far the material world advances, it cannot establish the happiness of mankind. Only when material and spiritual civilization are linked and coordinated will happiness be assured. Then material civilization will not contribute its energies to the forces of evil in destroying the oneness of humanity, for in material civilization good and evil advance together and maintain the same pace.

order.why: Confront the destructive uses of material achievement.
shortened: And among the teachings of Baha'u'llah is that although material civilization is one of the means for the progress of the world of mankind, yet until it becomes combined with Divine civilization, the desired result, which is the felicity of mankind, will not be attained. Consider! These battleships that reduce a city to ruins within the space of an hour are the result of material civilization; likewise the Krupp guns, the Mauser rifles, dynamite, submarines, torpedo boats, armed aircraft and bombers--all these weapons of war are the malignant fruits of material civilization.

order.why: Read the concrete encouragement of sciences and productive work.
Distinguish and connect the two calls to prosperity.
shortened: The one is the call of civilization, of the progress of the material world. This pertaineth to the world of phenomena, promoteth the principles of material achievement, and is the trainer for the physical accomplishments of mankind.
The propagator and executive power of this call is just government.

The other is the soul-stirring call of God, Whose spiritual teachings are safeguards of the everlasting glory, the eternal happiness and illumination of the world of humanity, and cause attributes of mercy to be revealed in the human world and the life beyond.
Its penetrative power is the Word of God.

Therefore, this civilization and material progress should be combined with the Most Great Guidance so that this nether world may become the scene of the appearance of the bestowals of the Kingdom, and physical achievements may be conjoined with the effulgences of the Merciful.

order.why: State the shared purpose of bettering the world.
shortened: All have been created for the betterment of the world.

order.why: Hear the call to develop cities and countries.
shortened: Promote ye the development of the cities of God and His countries, and glorify Him therein in the joyous accents of His well-favoured ones.

order.why: Consider counsel as an animating power.
shortened: Every man of insight will, in this day, readily admit that the counsels which the Pen of this Wronged One hath revealed constitute the supreme animating power for the advancement of the world and the exaltation of its peoples.

order.why: Read character, improvement, and learning from other peoples together.
shortened: By the Lord God, and there is no God but He, even the minutest details of civilized life derive from the grace of the Prophets of God. What thing of value to mankind has ever come into being which was not first set forth either directly or by implication in the Holy Scriptures?

They have not even grasped what is meant by the "imitation" referred to, nor do they know that the Divine religions enjoin upon and encourage all the faithful to adopt such principles as will conduce to continuous improvements, and to acquire from other peoples sciences and arts.

order.why: Bring the claim of belief into daily conduct.
shortened: They should justify their claim to be Baha'is by deeds and not by name. He is a true Baha'i who strives by day and by night to progress and advance along the path of human endeavour, whose most cherished desire is so to live and act as to enrich and illuminate the world, whose source of inspiration is the essence of divine virtue, whose aim in life is so to conduct himself as to be the cause of infinite progress. Only when he attains unto such perfect gifts can it be said of him that he is a true Baha'i.

order.why: Make the ethical dimension of civilization explicit.
shortened: Baha'u'llah teaches that material civilization is incomplete, insufficient and that divine civilization must be established. Material civilization concerns the world of matter or bodies, but divine civilization is the realm of ethics and moralities. Until the moral degree of the nations is advanced and human virtues attain a lofty level, happiness for mankind is impossible.

order.why: Read the distinction through body, spirit, and morals.
Consider the need for spiritual life.
shortened: Ninthly: Baha'u'llah taught that hearts must receive the Bounty of the Holy Spirit, so that Spiritual civilization may be established. For material civilization is not adequate for the needs of mankind and cannot be the cause of its happiness. Material civilization is like the body and spiritual civilization is like the soul. Body without soul cannot live.

order.why: Hear the related image of globe and light.
Read another expression of the glass and lamp.
Preserve the interviewer’s interruption within the dialogue.
Consider the reported priority given to finding the candle.
Read the image of body and spirit alongside fruitfulness.
shortened: Material civilization is likened to the body, whereas divine civilization is the spirit in that body. A body not manifesting the spirit is dead; a fruitless tree is worthless.

order.why: Recognize the founders and functions of both civilizations.
Join science and philosophy with moral education.
Distinguish the means of material and spiritual education.
Consider education through the cultivated garden.
Ask what ideals adults present to children.
shortened: The children of today are the citizens of tomorrow.  The mothers of today inculcate so many material ideas in the minds of their children.  They tell to the children in the way of encouragement: 'Study hard and thou shalt become the general of an army.'  They do not incite them in the acquirement of the ideal virtues.  They do not tell them:- 'Strive that thou mayst become a sincere, a just man; that thou mayst serve faithfully the world of humanity.'

order.why: Move toward a conference joining both kinds of virtue.
Read the appeal for moral and scientific advancement.
shortened: If a person studies all the sciences and arts, without heavenly Confirmations, he will not be able to accomplish very much. Now I hope you will become the Cause of moral and scientific advancement of all the Persians.

order.why: Set new inventions beside further spiritual possibilities.
shortened: This is the time for man to strive and put forth his greatest efforts in spiritual directions. Material civilization has reached an advanced plane, but now there is need of spiritual civilization. Material civilization alone will not satisfy; it cannot meet the conditions and requirements of the present age; its benefits are limited to the world of matter. There is no limitation to the spirit of man, for spirit in itself is progressive, and if the divine civilization be established, the spirit of man will advance.

order.why: Consider fuller reflection through human development.
shortened: The more the world of humanity develops, the more the effulgences or emanations of Divinity will become revealed, just as the stone, when it becomes polished and pure as a mirror, will reflect in fuller degree the glory and splendor of the sun.

order.why: Keep the concise distinction of two creations.
shortened: Know that creation is of two kinds: physical creation and spiritual creation.

order.why: Read the perfections associated with divine civilization.
Hear the reported account of spiritual power.
Consider the proposed power of unity.
Examine conflict as evidence of an unfinished task.
Keep the reported warning about undiscovered power in context.
Read the moral critique of nature in its historical rhetoric.
Distinguish instrumental affection from love offered for God.
Picture the melting of prejudices and widening fellowship.
Gather character, peace, and human unity together.
Read the vision of enduring institutions.
Consider the commonwealth of spiritual life.
Hear the language of conscience and liberation.
Keep the reported appeal within its context of peaceful agreement.
Preserve the recorded address and its distinct speaking voice.
shortened: Therefore, I ask those of insight and sound mind: Is it not true that the powers of material knowledge in this century have overcome the spiritual heart forces?
I know the reason to be the lack of a spiritual object, because the weak religion of our ancestors is no longer sufficient.

order.why: Read the assessment made during the journey west.
Hear a hope for spiritual forces to animate prosperity.
shortened: While it is true that its people have attained a marvelous material civilization, I hope that spiritual forces may animate this great body and a corresponding spiritual civilization be established.

order.why: Consider the call to complement material progress.
shortened: America and Europe have achieved the utmost progress in material civilization and are advancing day by day. It is hoped that divine civilization will also be established in these countries - that is, the civilization that the divine Prophets established, which pertains to the world of morals and spiritual education and is the cause of the spiritual progress of humanity.

order.why: Explains the complementary contributions of material and spiritual civilization.
Read advancement as light joined to light.
shortened: You have truly been progressive along material lines. The time has come to found and promulgate the spiritual civilization, and this divine civilization is no other than the teachings of the Prophets, so that the body and spirit may both keep up advancement and become as light on light.

order.why: Hear the reported concern about uneven development.
Retain the historical comparison of Western achievements.
shortened: Although the Western nations have perfected the machinery of natural civilization yet they are far left behind in divine civilization.

order.why: Read the image of obscurity beneath Paris’s brilliance.
Keep the landscape observation within its travel setting.
Distinguish questions about prosperity from the reply about virtues.
shortened: But some people ask me, 'Is your country developed? Is it prosperous and has it good trees, sweet fruits, beautiful animals and swift Arabian horses?'
But I speak to them of the trees of the world of existence, of the fruits of human virtues and of heavenly morals and traits and call people to the Kingdom of God.

order.why: Read the address to a spiritual youth in Japan.
shortened: O thou spiritual youth!
Japan hath made wonderful progress in material civilization, but she will become perfect when she also becometh spiritually developed and the power of the Kingdom becometh manifest in her.

order.why: Consider the hope for New York as a city of love.
shortened: As New York has made such progress in material civilization, I hope that it may also advance spiritually in the Kingdom and Covenant of God so that the friends here may become the cause of the illumination of America, that this city may become the city of love and that the fragrances of God may be spread from this place to all parts of the world.

order.why: Explore the proposed exchange between East and West.
Connect that exchange with ideals enacted materially.
Hear the concise affirmation of both forms of progress.
Read the surviving statement about coordinated public endeavor.
Hear the invitation to take a different direction.
shortened: For six thousand years we have been walking on the left-hand path; let us walk on the right-hand path now. We have passed many centuries in darkness, let us advance towards the light.

order.why: Distinguish passing satisfaction from spiritual peace.
shortened: Apparently some people may conceive that this is the height of happiness but it is material and fleeting. It does not last. The only abiding happiness is spiritual and ideal. That is real, all others are phantasmal and non-essential. The joy of the spirit confers Peace.

order.why: Read the statement of enduring human possibilities.
Read the contrast between passing constructions and enduring divine institutions.
Consider the reported contrast between two kinds of palace.
Close the linked readings with an ambition for earthly life.
Retain the supplied account of the two civilizations.
End with the supplied institutional perspective from Shoghi Effendi.
Consider the hope for the renewal of Persia.

questions: What does the lamp-and-light image help explain about civilization, and where might the analogy need further thought?
How could the same technical capacity serve human happiness or intensify suffering?
What would coordinated material and spiritual education involve in a school, profession, or community?
How does the Analects comparison illuminate moral leadership, and where do the two texts frame authority differently?
How might the historical appeal for an exchange between East and West be explored without treating either region as uniform?
What changes in institutions and everyday conduct would make the betterment of the world a practical measure of progress?

references.label: 1 · Analects II.3 · Government and the cultivation of virtue
references.note: The English text in The Chinese Classics contrasts people avoiding punishment under legal regulation with people developing moral awareness under leadership by virtue and propriety. Compare this distinction with the compilation’s concern for just government and moral education. Confucius’s account has its own setting and vocabulary; the comparison invites inquiry into the relationship between outward order and inward disposition.

subjects.displayTitle: Motion and growth: what it means to advance
subjects.introduction: A tiny, regular movement inside a clock is enough to tell the hours of the sun itself; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks what a comparable stirring in human consciousness might set in motion. His teaching that nothing in existence stays at rest is not a mere observation about physics. Growth and decline, the flower coming into being and fading, the earth turning, a child unfolding the qualities of the spirit, the ignorant becoming wise: each is a kind of motion, and the test of life is whether something still moves. Yet not every change is an advance, for there is change that raises and change that lowers, and a tree is allowed a long time to ripen because wisdom requires gradual development. Stillness has its own place when movement and rest alike are centred on a single point. Aristotle’s account of motion as potential becoming actual gives a precise vocabulary for sorting these kinds of change [1]. The thread continues into the relation of heat and motion, the continual renewal of creation, the arcs of ascent and descent, and finally spiritual transformation, where the question of direction matters most.
subjects.arc: Begin with a small movement and its consequences, distinguish the many kinds of change, and return to purposeful growth held together with patience.

order.why: Introduce natural change through the growing and fading flower.
shortened: Know that nothing that exists remains in a state of repose--that is, all things are in motion. They are either growing or declining, either coming from non-existence into existence or passing from existence into non-existence. So this flower, this hyacinth, was for a time coming from non-existence into existence and is now passing from existence into non-existence. This is called essential or natural motion, and it can in no wise be dissociated from created things, for it is one of their essential requirements, just as it is an essential requirement of fire to burn.

order.why: Open with the clock and a movement of consciousness.
shortened: Consider the clock, which, though a lifeless object, made of mere metal, by virtue of its order and skilled design is possessed of a highly regular movement. Though it is an inanimate object, it can determine the time cycles of the glorious sun itself.
A mighty outcome as this can result when a tiny and delicate movement appeareth in a heavy object.

Shouldst the movement of a spiritual yearning, which is like unto the spirit of this physical world, appear in the body of man, consider what manifest fruits and luminous perfections shall come forth! Therefore beseech God that through the divine means and spiritual powers, He may cause a movement in the consciousness of the human beings, and that thou mayest become like unto a timepiece for the movement of the stars of the Concourse on High and the celestial bodies of the All Glorious Kingdom and, even as a victorious spirit, become the means through which the body of this contingent world is moved and stirred.

order.why: Join movement and stillness around one purpose.
Make room for gradual development.
Read the reported distinctions among types of motion.
shortened: There are different degrees of motion. There is a motion of transit, that is from place to place. For example, the revolution of the earth around the sun; a bird flies from branch to branch. Another kind is the motion of inherent growth, like that of man from the condition of childhood to the estate of manhood, or the development of a tree from the seedling to its full fruition. The third is the motion of condition - the sick man passes from the stage of sickness to the state of health. The fourth motion is that of the spirit.
The fifth is the motion of the intellect whereby the ignorant become wise; the indifferent, alert; the dark, illuminated and the carnally-minded, spiritual.

order.why: Distinguish change that elevates from change that diminishes.
shortened: There are two kinds of changes and alterations. One causes descent and one ascent. The one which causes descent is not good, but on the contrary. The other change, which causes ascent, is acceptable.
The mineral carbon changes in many stations until diamonds are produced from it.

order.why: Observe the sequence of seasons and days.
Consider the wisdom expressed through changing conditions.
shortened: For example, if the Most Great Luminary of the horizons were to remain perpetually rising at the meridian circle, all generated beings, contingent things and visible realities would be burned up and destroyed. No spring would remain, nor flower garden, no tree or fruit, no summer or autumn, no April or October, no birds or living creatures or humans. It is therefore evident that these are signs of wisdom.

order.why: Hear the broad claim about motion and existence.
shortened: Absolute repose does not exist in nature.
Thus it is evident that movement is essential to all existence.

We have seen that movement is essential to existence; nothing that has life is without motion. All creation, whether of the mineral, vegetable or animal kingdom, is compelled to obey the law of motion; it must either ascend or descend.

order.why: Read inherent and derivative motion together.
Retain the concise statement about creation’s movement.
shortened: O Adib! The world of creation is in motion and movement.

order.why: Consider movement as a mirror of bounty.
shortened: The world of existence is in motion and movement, and the world of creation is a mirror of the favors of the All-Merciful Lord.

order.why: Extend the discussion to thought and consciousness.
Read the moving sea alongside the waves of mind.
Hear the reported examples of motion in nature.
shortened: Motion is the sign of life. If there be no wind, no motion the air becomes impure. When water is stagnant it also becomes impure. There is motion in everything, all the plants are moving. All bodies whether large or small are moving. There is no globe which is absolutely stationary. The people thought that the poles were without motion. In reality there are two motions: rotation and revolutions.

order.why: Follow the examples into condition, maturity, and attraction.
shortened: There are other kinds of motion. One is a local motion, which is dependent upon condition. For example, the turning of wine into vinegar. A second is an essential motion, such as when the body of man develops into maturity. Another is a spiritual motion, which is the attraction of the hearts.

order.why: Keep the historical cosmology and spiritual application distinct.
shortened: The point is this: that all existing things (creation) are in motion. Therefore it is known that motion is the cause of life and lack of motion is indicative of decay or retrogression.

But the main motion is based upon the holy books which give life to man and lifts him from a miserable stage to that of exaltation. It moves man from the center of eternal degradation to the center of eternal life. This is the real and important motion.

order.why: Consider atoms within the reported account of progression.
Retain the reported statement about elemental transformation.
Read the dynamo image within its historical account.
shortened: All material things are ordered like a planetary system. In the center is the divine dynamo and around Him circle in a raving dance the matter particles, the so-called atoms. The faster the movement, the firmer and denser appears the matter to us.

order.why: Keep ethereal power within the source’s natural philosophy.
Read the historical experiment as a reported illustration.
Preserve the attribution of the atomic account to al-Ashari.
shortened: Al-Ash'ari says about it: [']The entire creation consists of matter and power (movement). Matter, the corporeal, consists of atoms which are alike; they, the atoms, fill up space, they are units without magnitude conceived as points, on which all spatial corporeal existence is based. The atoms do not penetrate into each other, they move, they change. All changes of the atoms are based on combination and separation, on quick and undetectable movement -on this is dependent the form, the appearance of the body.

order.why: Notice the account of the ten intellects is expressly challenged.
shortened: These ten intellects are Aristotle's concept. For example, [he says] motion is of two kinds: forced motion and circular motion. Circular motion is evidence of will. Since we observe circular motion in these spheres, they possess will, and therefore in these spheres there exists an intellectual force which is the governing force of that sphere.
This is but imagination.
Now it is known that all motion is compelled motion. This sun is compelled to move, even these other spheres are compelled to move. All motion is compelled, not volitional.

order.why: Turn to the relationship between motion and order.
Read the reported examples of localized powers.
Consider a related explanation of centers.
Follow the analogy from a center to spiritual influence.
Consider the direction of attention toward a center of light.
shortened: The lights of earth are all acceptable, but the center of effulgence is the sun, and we must direct our gaze to the sun. God is the Supreme Center. The more we turn toward this Center of Light, the greater will be our capacity.

order.why: Read the Word of God as a center of illumination.
Enter the extended metaphysical language of the Divine Soul.
shortened: And as for "the Divine Soul" (an-nafs al-ilahiyyah), it consists of the Universal Reality which brings together all of the Divine realities of the realm of Primal Manifestation (lahutiyyah) and the eternal secrets, the outer aspect of which is the ancient light and the inner aspect is the most mighty and sublime mystery, the Primal Point from which appear all things and to which they revert, from which they originate and to which they return.
And so the horizons and souls become filled and illumined by it on the Day of the Covenant, and on account of it the tabernacles of unity tremble and are set in motion.

order.why: Hear creation and movement in the language of praise.
Consider the relation of stillness and motion in revelation.
Read motion’s dependence upon divine sustenance.
shortened: Thou hadst asked about the motion and rest of things - whether they are by God's will. This is certainly so, for the sustenance of existence comes from the All-Bountiful. If sustenance from God did not reach existence, no created thing would move.

order.why: Distinguish movement through the Word from familiar classifications.
shortened: O thou who advancest toward the Supreme Horizon! Be moved by the motion apparent from the heat of God's compelling Word, which God hath made sanctified from the three motions which are the six and what is above them of the motions mentioned in the books of the people. Thus doth the Lord of all beings command thee. And this motion, though it revolveth around itself, yet it hath motions which none knoweth save thy Lord, the Mighty, the All-Knowing.

order.why: Hear the summons to movement through divine utterance.
Connect the heat of love with joining friends.
shortened: O friend! The cause of motion is heat, and the cause of ascension is lightness. God willing, the fire of the love of God which is deposited in thy verses will become the cause of ascension and the reason for motion, and will unite the friends with the friends.

order.why: Read love as movement toward the center.
shortened: O servant of Baha! Be self-sacrificing in the path of God, and wing thy flight unto the heavens of the love of the Abha Beauty, for any movement animated by love moveth from the periphery to the centre, from space to the Day-Star of the universe.

Perchance thou deemest this to be difficult, but I tell thee that such cannot be the case, for when the motivating and guiding power is the divine force of magnetism it is possible, by its aid, to traverse time and space easily and swiftly.

order.why: Consider the reassurance of purposeful spiritual influence.
shortened: O thou who warmest thyself by the fire of the love of God, spreading from the Tree of the Covenant! Let thy soul be at ease and thy heart in peace concerning the perfect success and progress which the pen is not able to express, for in a short time thou shalt see the flag of the Kingdom waving in those far and wide regions, and the lights of the Truth shining brilliantly in its dawn above those horizons, and thou shalt know that thou art the center of the circle of the love of God, the axis around which souls revolve in their way and supplication to God.

order.why: Distinguish natural movement from will and choice.
Distinguishes voluntary and involuntary motion within the movement of creation.
Keep the reported account of ascent and descent in context.
Read the progression described across degrees of spirit.
Consider progress without a final boundary.
Ask how a season of growth is received.
Read the personal observation about remaining in one place.
shortened: When staying and residing in one place continues for long, inevitably some weariness results.

You are right - all created things are in motion, and through this universal motion the order of the world of existence is maintained. If any created thing becomes fixed in one place and ceases from motion, decline inevitably occurs. The breeze must constantly blow, the sea must have waves and motion, the stars must transit through the constellations.

order.why: Keep the counsel to travel within its addressed circumstances.
shortened: Motion is one of the essential requirements of the realities of beings and the cause of attaining universal benefits in the world of creation.

Therefore it is better that one attain essential motion, seek existential motion, desire qualitative motion, attain material motion and seek spiritual motion. All these motions are the cause of deliverance. Therefore if you are traveling and in motion it is certainly better than being lifeless, sluggish, melancholy and tormented in one place.

order.why: Hear the bird analogy as an appeal to continued growth.
Read the related warning about ceasing to advance.
Turn that image into daily reflection.
shortened: Day by day he must endeavor to become better, his belief must increase and become firmer, his good qualities and his turning to God must be greater, the fire of his love must flame more brightly; then day by day he will make progress, for to stop advancing is the means of going back. The bird when he flies soars ever higher and higher, for as soon as he stops flying he will come down. Every day, in the morning when arising you should compare today with yesterday and see in what condition you are.

order.why: Consider the call to progress in every world.
shortened: Man must always advance. As soon as man remains stationary in a certain cause he will go backward. Therefore he must strive that man may advance day by day, that he may progress in all the worlds.

order.why: Close the linked readings with the relation of life and movement.
Retain the supplied statement on motion as essential to existence.
Consider the limits of circling within one’s own understanding.
Read the supplied image of sincere intention as attraction.
Consider the philosophical image of the soul around its center.
End with the supplied counterpoint of contemplative stillness.

questions: How does distinguishing movement in place, growth, changed condition, and spiritual transformation affect your reading?
What makes a change an advance rather than simply a different state?
How can the appeals to keep moving be read alongside the passage about the wisdom of gradual development?
What does Aristotle’s account of potential becoming actual clarify, and what remains different in the devotional uses of motion?
How do attribution and historical context help when a passage reports a cosmological theory or challenges someone else’s explanation?
What might it mean to center both movement and stillness on one purpose, and how does the final philosophical counterpoint complicate the inquiry?

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Physics III.1 · Motion and potential
references.note: In the translation by R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye, Aristotle analyzes motion in relation to potentiality and actuality, distinguishing change in quality, quantity, and place. His examples include building, learning, ripening, and ageing. Compare this conceptual inquiry with the compilation’s varied uses of movement, while keeping metaphysical argument, physical illustration, and spiritual exhortation distinguishable.

subjects.displayTitle: Divine good pleasure: grace and the life of deeds
subjects.introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá turns a lofty phrase on its head: the good pleasure of God, He says, resides in our being pleased with His servants. The approval of heaven is pulled down into kitchens and meetings and the way we speak of one another. Bahá’u’lláh adds a harder word. A person might wash the feet of all mankind and still carry no fragrance of acceptance if the deeds were set as snares to catch a reward. Effort matters, but it is not a currency; faith is a token of grace rather than a wage of justice, and the mirror cannot wipe away its own dust. The Letter to the Ephesians holds the same tension when it calls salvation a gift and in the next breath describes a life created for good works [1]. To live toward divine good pleasure is to examine one’s conduct and lean one’s hope on mercy. The road runs on into forgiveness and the compassion of God, into the saying that many are called but few are chosen, and into paradise as nearness.
subjects.arc: Begin with relationships and conduct, explore the gift that sustains effort, and approach acceptance and paradise through humility and hope.

order.why: Challenge deeds treated as a means of securing reward.
shortened: How many a man hath secluded himself in the climes of India, denied himself the things that God hath decreed as lawful, imposed upon himself austerities and mortifications, and hath not been remembered by God, the Revealer of Verses. Make not your deeds as snares wherewith to entrap the object of your aspiration, and deprive not yourselves of this Ultimate Objective for which have ever yearned all such as have drawn nigh unto God. Say: The very life of all deeds is My good pleasure, and all things depend upon Mine acceptance.

order.why: Open with good pleasure in relation to other people.
shortened: I for one have not succeeded; God willing, thou mayest succeed and pray in turn for my success. For the good-pleasure of God and that of His servants are the greatest of divine bestowals; indeed God’s good-pleasure resideth in our being pleased with His servants.

order.why: Make the search a question of conduct and circumstance.
Join acceptance with acting upon guidance.
shortened: The foundation of all deeds is the good-pleasure of God, and His good-pleasure is not attained except through acting according to what He hath commanded in His Book.

order.why: Read enduring value through conduct and divine pleasure.
shortened: That which remains lasting and enduring for man is the good-pleasure of the Lord God and conduct and behavior in accordance with the teachings of the Forgiving One.

order.why: Hear the counsel to act accordingly.
shortened: Hearken unto the divine counsel and act in accordance with that wherefrom the sweet-smelling savor of His good-pleasure may be inhaled. If thou attainest unto this exalted and most high station, thou shalt be blessed with the word of His good-pleasure from the Lord of Names.

order.why: Consider its application to great and small affairs.
shortened: A Baha'i must conform all his great and small affairs in accord with the good-pleasure of the Blessed Perfection. This is the unerring criterion.

order.why: Read acceptance alongside holding fast to the Book.
Consider a life directed toward truth.
Hear the insistence on what animates virtuous acts.
Read the related image of the spirit of deeds.
shortened: The spirit of all deeds is the good-pleasure of God, for if one should perform all good deeds, yet from them the fragrance of God's good-pleasure be not inhaled, those deeds will yield neither fruit nor effect nor result.

order.why: Consider dependence upon divine acceptance.
shortened: For all things are dependent upon His Will, and the worth of all acts is conditioned upon His acceptance and pleasure. The whole universe is but a handful of clay in His grasp.

order.why: Read the fasting prayer’s emphasis on divine sovereignty.
shortened: For the doings of men are all dependent upon Thy good-pleasure, and are conditioned by Thy behest. Shouldst Thou regard him who hath broken the fast as one who hath observed it, such a man would be reckoned among them who from eternity had been keeping the fast. And shouldst Thou decree that he who hath observed the fast hath broken it, that person would be numbered with such as have caused the Robe of Thy Revelation to be stained with dust, and been far removed from the crystal waters of this living Fountain.

order.why: Explore acceptance through recognition of the Manifestation.
shortened: For in all deeds performed by anyone in his life, he desireth naught but the good pleasure of God, inasmuch as this is the uttermost end of all. But it is undoubtedly true that the good pleasure of God shall not be manifested save through the good pleasure of the One unto Whom God hath conferred His supreme testimony.

order.why: Introduce mercy that precedes the servant’s turning.
shortened: Thou art, in truth, He Whose mercy hath encompassed all the worlds, and whose grace hath embraced all that dwell on earth and in heaven. Who is there that hath cried after Thee, and whose prayer hath remained unanswered?
I bear witness that Thou hadst turned toward Thy servants ere they had turned toward Thee, and hadst remembered them ere they had remembered Thee.

order.why: Consider the candle and mirror’s need for assistance.
shortened: Neither the candle nor the lamp can be lighted through their own unaided efforts, nor can it ever be possible for the mirror to free itself from its dross. It is clear and evident that until a fire is kindled the lamp will never be ignited, and unless the dross is blotted out from the face of the mirror it can never represent the image of the sun nor reflect its light and glory.

order.why: Let the prayer speak from despair toward hope.
shortened: In the darksome night of despair, my eye turneth expectant and full of hope to the morn of Thy boundless favor and at the hour of dawn my drooping soul is refreshed and strengthened in remembrance of Thy beauty and perfection. He whom the grace of Thy mercy aideth, though he be but a drop, shall become the boundless ocean, and the merest atom which the outpouring of Thy loving-kindness assisteth, shall shine even as the radiant star.

order.why: Hear the broken-winged bird’s petition.
Read freedom from desire as requiring grace.
shortened: Man cannot free himself from the onslaught of vain and selfish desires save through the confirming grace of the Holy Spirit.

order.why: Consider the distinction between acquired knowledge and faith as gift.
shortened: For faith, which is life eternal, is a token of grace and not the result of justice. The flame of the fire of love, in this world of earth and water, burns by the power of attraction and not through human effort and striving, although through the latter one may indeed acquire knowledge, learning, and other perfections. It is the light of the divine Beauty, then, that must stir up and move the spirit through its attractive power. Wherefore is it said: "many are called, but few are chosen".

order.why: Hear gratitude for guidance received.
shortened: This plenty is a special favor bestowed by a loving God, these are blessings and rare gifts deriving from His grace. In the Gospel He saith: "For many are called, but few are chosen." That is, to many is it offered, but rare is the soul who is singled out to receive the great bestowal of guidance. "Such is the bounty of God: to whom He will He giveth it, and of immense bounty is God."

order.why: Read the contrast between austerity and unearned acceptance.
shortened: O ye peoples of the Kingdom! How many a soul expended all its span of life in worship, endured the mortification of the flesh, longed to gain an entry into the Kingdom, and yet failed, while ye, with neither toil nor pain nor self-denial, have won the prize and entered in.

order.why: Consider mercy as a freely bestowed gift.
shortened: O ye loved ones of God! Is there any giver save God? He singleth out for His mercy whomsoever He willeth.

order.why: Hear recognition described through divine favor.
shortened: Whomsoever Thou willest Thou causest to draw nigh unto the Most Great Ocean, and on whomsoever Thou desirest Thou conferrest the honor of recognizing Thy Most Ancient Name.

order.why: Read the reported account of illuminating bounty.
shortened: God's eternal Mercy is immeasurable. He has always chosen certain souls upon whom He has shed the Divine Bounty of His heart, whose minds He has illumined with celestial light, to whom He has revealed the sacred mysteries, and kept clear before their sight the Mirror of Truth.

order.why: Consider spiritual life as proceeding from God.
shortened: Hence it is clear and evident that the holy reality---the true existence---of every great man proceeds from God and owes its being to the breath of the Holy Spirit.

order.why: Read the dependence of lasting perfections upon divine power.
shortened: These gifts, however, do not manifest themselves in the reality of man save through a celestial and divine power and through the heavenly teachings, for they require a supernatural power. Traces of these perfections may well appear in the world of nature, but they are as fleeting and ephemeral as rays of sunlight upon the wall.

order.why: Distinguish the rational soul and divine assistance.
shortened: The human spirit refers to the rational soul by which humans are distinguished from animals. It is not from the realm of physical elements but rather from spiritual substances that are not subject to corruption.

The divine spirit which is from God's command refers to the holy power, divine confirmations, eternal assistance, divine knowledge and heavenly sciences with which God aids whomever He wishes among His righteous servants. Through it they attain spiritual unveilings and certain visions, and they achieve complete, precedent mercy and abundant grace.

order.why: Consider the human spirit through the image of receptive soil.
shortened: The spirit of man must acquire its bounties from the Kingdom of God in order that it may become the mirror and manifestation of lights and the dawning point of divine traces, because the human reality is like the soil.

Similarly, the human spirit or reality of man, unless it becomes the recipient of the lights of the Kingdom, develops divine susceptibilities and consciously reflects the effulgence of God, will not be the manifestation of ideal bounties, for only the reality of man can become the mirror wherein the lights of God are revealed.

order.why: Read the need for assistance in a great undertaking.
shortened: It is clear, however, that mere human power is incapable of fulfilling this great office, and that the results of human thought alone cannot secure such bounties. How can a single person, with no aid or assistance, lay the foundations of such a lofty edifice? A divine and spiritual power is therefore needed to enable him to carry out this mission.

order.why: Consider the counsel to seekers of truth.
shortened: O thou maid-servant of God! The aim of the theosophists is to attain to Truth, but the Truth is unattainable except through the favor of the Holy Spirit. The light hath a center and if one desire to seek it otherwise but from the center, he can never attain to it.

order.why: Hold searching, longing, knowledge, and grace together.
shortened: Inasmuch as it hath been clearly shown that only those who are initiated into the divine mysteries can comprehend the melodies uttered by the Bird of Heaven, it is therefore incumbent upon every one to seek enlightenment from the illumined in heart and from the Treasuries of divine mysteries regarding the intricacies of God's Faith and the abstruse allusions in the utterances of the Daysprings of Holiness. Thus will these mysteries be unraveled, not by the aid of acquired learning, but solely through the assistance of God and the outpourings of His grace.

Only when the lamp of search, of earnest striving, of longing desire, of passionate devotion, of fervid love, of rapture, and ecstasy, is kindled within the seeker's heart, and the breeze of His loving-kindness is wafted upon his soul, will the darkness of error be dispelled, the mists of doubts and misgivings be dissipated, and the lights of knowledge and certitude envelop his being.

order.why: Read the invitation to study existence and scripture.
Keep rapid spiritual passage dependent on confirmation.
shortened: 87 These journeys have no visible ending in this temporal world, but the detached wayfarer-should invisible confirmation descend upon him and the Guardian of the Cause assist him-may traverse these seven stages in seven steps, nay rather in seven breaths, nay even in a single breath, should God will and desire it.

order.why: Consider opportunity and the response it invites.
Join effort with continuing supplication.
shortened: Forever supplicate and entreat at the court of Majesty and beg confirmation and assistance. Make ye an effort that you may win the good pleasure of Baha'u'llah. All the natural and supernatural advancements in the human world revolve around this one problem.

order.why: Hear the appeal to receive available mercy.
Ask for inspiration in remembrance itself.
Read the extended petition for protection and return.
Approach alignment of desire through prayer.
shortened: O God, my God! Look not upon my hopes and my doings, nay rather look upon Thy will that hath encompassed the heavens and the earth. By Thy Most Great Name, O Thou Lord of all nations! I have desired only what Thou didst desire, and love only what Thou dost love.

order.why: Hear trust and submission in their devotional voice.
shortened: Ask whatsoever thou wishest of Him alone; seek whatsoever thou seekest from Him alone.

With a look He granteth a hundred thousand hopes, with a glance He healeth a hundred thousand incurable ills, with a nod He layeth balm on every wound, with a glimpse He freeth the hearts from the shackles of grief.

He doeth as He doeth, and what recourse have we? He carrieth out His Will, He ordaineth what He pleaseth. Then better for thee to bow down thy head in submission, and put thy trust in the All-Merciful Lord.

order.why: Read the difficulty of separation within the language of friendship.
shortened: Grievous is it for the Friend to be separated from the friend, yet the Friend hath so desired. What befitteth the friend is submission to, and contentment with, the good-pleasure of the Friend. The Friend saith: "My friend, thou wilt surely love that which I love." Therefore, be thou content with the good-pleasure of the Friend and with whatsoever proceedeth from Him.

order.why: Consider contentment with the divine will.
